solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Time to spoil 9's game?

indicators.note: to spoil something is to mess it up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: 9 here is read as the number nine, so 9's gives the plural NINES

explanation.surface: A spoiler wrecking the game of whoever is clued at 9 across.
explanation.walkthrough: '9's' looks like a cross-reference to another clue, but it is just the number: NINES, which 'spoil' turns into ENNIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn tennis is a racket sport, a game; the question mark signals the definition by example.

clue.text: Being economical with the truth, criminally libels FT

definitions.note: a participle phrase standing for the verb phrase; telling small lies is being economical with the truth

indicators.note: acting criminally means acting wrongly, so the letters are rearranged out of their proper order

explanation.surface: Someone libelling the Financial Times is lying, and criminally so.
explanation.definitionFit: Being economical with the truth is a famous euphemism for lying, and minor lies are fibs.

clue.text: Returning to write melody, one by Holst?

indicators.note: returning means going back, so the word for to write is read backwards

parts.note: to pen is to write
a melody is a tune

explanation.surface: A composer goes back to writing melodies, perhaps like Holst.
explanation.walkthrough: Holst wrote The Planets suite; one of its movements is named after this planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Holst's orchestral suite The Planets includes a movement for each planet, this one the mystic.

clue.text: Frost admitting "I like a drink"

indicators.note: admitting means confessing out loud, so what is spoken is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: to sup is to drink, so 'I like a drink' becomes I SUP

explanation.surface: Somebody named Frost confesses to enjoying a tipple.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, I SUP (eye-sup) sounds just like the two words of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To become covered or blocked with ice is what frost does to windows and pipes.

clue.text: Gaze fixedly about space with glasses

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word is placed around the others

parts.note: to stare is to gaze fixedly
an em is a printer's space

explanation.surface: Someone stares into the distance while wearing spectacles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'glasses' suggests spectacles but means drinking vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: Stemmed drinking vessels such as wine flutes are collectively called this.

clue.text: When drunk, Cher Tweets "Hi, weird sisters"

indicators.note: a drunk person's words come out jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The singer Cher sends a tipsy greeting on social media to some strange sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: The Weird Sisters are the witches in Shakespeare's Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare calls the prophesying trio in Macbeth the Weird Sisters.

clue.text: Scottish family magazine including chapter upsetting Roger

indicators.note: including means containing, so the first word holds the second
upsetting means overturning, so the name is rearranged

explanation.surface: A Scottish family periodical runs a chapter that offends someone called Roger.
explanation.definitionFit: Clan Gregor's chiefs took this surname; it is a Highland clan.

clue.text: Everybody say "Romania!" quickly

parts.note: all means everybody
eg, for example, is what say means here
RO is Romania's international code

explanation.surface: A crowd all shouting the name of Romania in quick succession.
explanation.definitionFit: As a tempo marking in music, this Italian word directs a brisk, lively pace.

clue.text: Waugh visiting Kiev, Ely, Naples

indicators.note: visiting means calling in on, so the answer is found inside the place names

explanation.surface: Waugh on a tour of Kiev, Ely and Naples.
explanation.walkthrough: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Waugh, author of Brideshead Revisited, had this first name.

clue.text: Backsliding Liberal Democrat: "Recess? Get stuffed!"

indicators.note: to be stuffed is to be filled, so the outer pair receives the recess word inside

parts.note: LD is short for Liberal Democrat, a UK party
an apse is a recess in a church

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat politician rudely dismisses a call for a parliamentary recess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get stuffed!' reads as an insult but tells you to put APSE inside L D.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone backsliding has fallen away from former standards, as a lapsed believer has.

clue.text: Spooner's runny French cheese … man, packed a helluva punch

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the starts of words, so the opening sounds of the two words change places

parts.note: a runny cheese is loose
brie is a soft French cheese

explanation.surface: A runny cheese described as packing a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of LOOSE BRIE to hear BROOSE LEE.
explanation.definitionFit: The martial-arts film star was famed for his one-inch punch, a fighting man.

clue.text: The old dromedary/camel question posed by acting mother?

definitions.text: The old dromedary/camel question posed by acting mother?

parts.words: The old dromedary/camel question posed by acting mother?
parts.note: a dromedary has one hump and a camel two; the person who says 'I'll be mother' pours the tea and asks about sugar

explanation.surface: A puzzle about telling camels apart, posed by someone playing mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll be mother' is a British phrase meaning 'I'll pour the tea'; the pourer asks how much sugar you want.
explanation.definitionFit: The standard tea-pourer's question about sugar cubes, punning on the humps of the two beasts.

clue.text: 4d united in favour of the VP

definitions.note: d is the symbol for an old British penny

indicators.note: in places the letter for united inside the word meaning in favour of

parts.note: for means in favour of, with 'in' doing double duty
Mike Pence was US Vice-President when the puzzle appeared

explanation.surface: Something about a deal united behind the US Vice-President.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does double duty, as part of 'in favour of' and as the signal to insert U.
explanation.definitionFit: Before decimal currency, d stood for pennies, so 4d was a sum of four old pennies.

clue.text: Public school's 50/50 to make the game

parts.note: A famous English public school, with the 's giving the S
evens are odds of 50/50 in betting

explanation.surface: A public school's even split producing a sport.
explanation.walkthrough: Rugby School is the public school where rugby football is said to have begun.
explanation.definitionFit: A seven-a-side form of rugby union, played in short matches, is a sport.

clue.text: Meat dish (hopefully not as tough as old boots)

definitions.text: Meat dish (hopefully not as tough as old boots)

parts.words: Meat dish (hopefully not as tough as old boots)
parts.note: the dish shares its name with wellington boots, so one hopes it is not as tough as old boots

explanation.surface: A diner hopes the meat is tender.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellingtons are rubber boots, so the old-boots jibe plays on the dish's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Fillet steak wrapped in pastry is a classic roast meat dish named after a duke.

clue.text: Lewis isn't broadcast in places where Bergerac might be shown

definitions.text: places where Bergerac might be shown

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered about, so the letters are spread into a new order

explanation.surface: TV detective Lewis is not aired where Bergerac is screened.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis and Bergerac were British TV detective series; Bergerac is also a French wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant's lists of bottles are where a Bergerac wine would appear.

clue.text: Poor Keith Moon's last Kansas get-together for the band

indicators.note: poor means badly made, so the name is jumbled
last points to the final letter of Moon

parts.note: KS is the postal abbreviation for Kansas

explanation.surface: A tribute get-together for the late Who drummer Keith Moon.
explanation.walkthrough: Keith Moon was the drummer of the Who, misdirecting toward that band; 'get-together' just assembles the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The sixties rock group behind You Really Got Me is a band.

clue.text: Order two more gnocchi — it's good for business

indicators.note: to order is to arrange, so the letters are put in a new sequence

explanation.surface: A diner orders extra gnocchi, which is good for the restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanding economy, measured by rising output, benefits commerce.

clue.text: Hearse transporting ex-PM's body

indicators.note: transporting means carrying, so the vehicle holds the name inside

parts.note: a hearse is a car
Dave is David Cameron, a former UK Prime Minister

explanation.surface: A hearse carrying a former Prime Minister's remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A corpse, especially one used for dissection, is a dead body.

clue.text: Wife called; left message, ending in noisy argument

parts.note: rang means telephoned, called

indicators.note: ending points to the final letter of the word message

explanation.surface: A wife phoned and left a message that ended in a shouting match.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, loud dispute is a wrangle; the verb also means to quarrel.

clue.text: I had dinner after King Duncan finally got stabbed

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of Duncan

parts.note: to have dinner is to be fed

explanation.surface: After dinner, King Duncan was stabbed, as in Macbeth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' is a link in answer order: the K and N pieces come before I FED.
explanation.definitionFit: Being attacked with a blade is being knifed, a synonym for stabbed.

clue.text: In Barcelona, Dali is an acknowledged genius

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the answer is found inside the two words

explanation.surface: Salvador Dali, the Catalan artist, is hailed as a genius in Barcelona.
explanation.walkthrough: Dali seems to be the genius, but the genius is the tennis player Rafael Nadal.
explanation.definitionFit: Rafael Nadal, a Spanish tennis great with many Grand Slam titles, is widely hailed as a genius.

clue.text: Nose to tail Channel port vehicle queue had a few too many

indicators.note: nose to tail means the front letter moves to the back

parts.note: Dover is an English port on the Channel
a taxi rank is a queue of vehicles

explanation.surface: A queue of traffic, nose to tail at Dover, drinks too much while waiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nose to tail' sounds like traffic but moves D from the front of DOVER to its end, giving OVERD.
explanation.definitionFit: Drinking more than is wise is overdoing it, just as a few too many does.

clue.text: "Doctor: I have reduced libido"

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, as in the contracted form 've

parts.note: the full word have

explanation.surface: A patient tells the doctor of a lowered sex drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced' shortens HAVE to VE, as in I've.
explanation.definitionFit: Sexual appetite is often called sex drive, so drive stands for libido.

clue.text: Grand Prix tops conserving energy, a test for 21 at 1 across

parts.note: Formula One, F1, is Grand Prix racing, with the 1 read as I

indicators.note: conserving means keeping, so the tops hold the letter inside

parts.note: vests are tops
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Motor racing tops that save energy, a test for a tennis player.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 is NADAL and 1 across is TENNIS: a men's Grand Slam match can go to five sets.
explanation.definitionFit: Men's Grand Slam matches are best of five sets, the toughest test of endurance.

clue.text: Tabloid featuring nine grand revolver

indicators.note: featuring means having inside, so the paper holds the other letters

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
IX is nine in Roman numerals
G is a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A tabloid headline about a nine-thousand-pound revolver.
explanation.definitionFit: A revolver with six chambers is called a six-shooter or six-gun.

clue.text: In retirement Blofeld became a father, getting ridicule

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: Blofeld is Number One of SPECTRE in the Bond stories, NO I
sired means fathered

explanation.surface: Bond villain Blofeld retires and becomes a dad, only to be mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In retirement' reverses NO I + SIRED; Blofeld is SPECTRE's Number One in the Bond stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Scornful mockery of someone is derision, the same as ridicule.
